```{r setup}
#| include: false
source(here::here("R", "area_report_helpers.R"))
X    <- readRDS(here::here("data", "area_sussex.rds"))            # R/17_area_analysis.R
TR   <- readRDS(here::here("data", "trust_effects.rds"))          # R/19_trust_effects.R
DE   <- readRDS(here::here("data", "district_effects.rds"))       # R/18_district_effects.R
LADS <- readRDS(here::here("data", "sussex_lads.rds"))            # R/19b_sussex_boundaries.R
LAS <- c("East Sussex", "West Sussex", "Brighton and Hove")
ALL <- c("Sussex", LAS)

S <- X$schools
NAT <- X$national
latest <- X$latest_panel
abs_last <- tail(X$abs_years, 1)
GOV <- gov_table(X, TR, DE, council = "the council") |>
  left_join(S |> transmute(URN = as.integer(URN), LANAME), by = "URN")

ap <- X$area_profile |> filter(year_label == latest)
prof <- X$profiles |> filter(year_label == latest)
p_at <- function(la) if (la == "Sussex") ap else prof |> filter(LANAME == la)

eff <- X$effects
e_at <- function(la, g) eff |> filter(la == !!la, group == g)
r27 <- function(out, la, spec) X$r27[[out]] |> filter(la == !!la, spec == !!spec) |> pull(rank)

dec <- X$decomp
d_get <- function(la, g, comp) dec$points[dec$la == la & dec$group == g & dec$component == comp]
d_tot <- function(la, g) { x <- dec |> filter(la == !!la, group == g) |> slice(1); x$la_att8 - x$nat_att8 }

ser <- X$abs_series
s_at <- function(area, tp, col = "abs_rate") ser[[col]][ser$area == area & ser$time_period == tp]
rk <- X$abs_ranks
rk_at <- function(la, tp) rk$rank_abs[rk$la_name == la & rk$time_period == tp]
ctx <- X$abs_context
c_at <- function(la) ctx |> filter(LANAME == la)

rs <- X$reasons |> filter(time_period == abs_last)
rs_w <- rs |> select(area, reason, pp) |> pivot_wider(names_from = area, values_from = pp)
r_at <- function(area, r) rs_w[[area]][rs_w$reason == r]

exa <- X$excl$area; ex_last <- max(exa$time_period)
ex_at <- function(a, col = "susp_rate") exa[[col]][exa$la_name == a & exa$time_period == ex_last]

js <- X$joint$schools
js_sx <- js |> filter(URN %in% X$urns)

# District summary: profile, four-year value added, and the district test
lp <- X$lad_profiles |> filter(year_label == latest, LANAME %in% LAS)
dva <- DE$sussex_va |> group_by(lad) |>
  summarise(va = mean(va), schools = n(), below = sum(va < 0), .groups = "drop")
dfe <- DE$focus |> filter(outcome == "All pupils") |>
  select(spec, lad, effect, sig) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = spec, values_from = c(effect, sig))
DIST <- lp |> select(lad, la = LANAME, att8, att8_dis, fsm, absence, ks2_c) |>
  left_join(dva, by = "lad") |> left_join(dfe, by = "lad")
```

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Draft for discussion

This review draws together the [East Sussex](east_sussex.html),
[West Sussex](west_sussex.html) and [Mid Sussex](mid_sussex.html)
documents, and the Brighton and Hove findings of
[How to Pull the Right Lever](https://adamdennett.github.io/school_attainment_tool/pulling_the_right_lever_v2.html).
Every figure comes from published Department for Education data and the
national models documented there. Nothing uses pupil-level records.
:::

# Summary {.unnumbered}

Sussex has `r nrow(S)` state-funded secondary schools across three local
authorities and thirteen districts. Taken together in `r latest`:

- **Results:** `r pts(ap$att8)` in Attainment 8, against
  `r pts(NAT$att8)` for England.
- **Disadvantaged pupils:** `r pts(ap$att8_dis)` against
  `r pts(NAT$att8_dis)`.
- **Disadvantage:** `r pp(ap$fsm)`% of pupils are disadvantaged, against
  `r pp(NAT$fsm)`% nationally.

Sussex is less disadvantaged than England, does a little less well
overall, and does markedly less well by its disadvantaged pupils. The
findings:

- **The disadvantaged shortfall is the region's shared problem.** Every
  one of the three authorities is below England for its disadvantaged
  pupils. The largest single cause is being in the South East
  (`r pts(-d_get("Sussex", "Disadvantaged", "Region"))` points). Of
  England's nine regions, the South East has the most negative regional
  effect for disadvantaged pupils. Absence and prior attainment add to
  it.
- **Beneath that, three different systems.**
  - *Brighton and Hove* has effective schools held back by absence far
    beyond what its intake predicts.
  - *East Sussex* has schools that do about what is expected, pupils with
    lower prior attainment, and the absence its intake predicts.
  - *West Sussex* has an advantaged intake, ordinary attendance, and
    schools below expectation, most of all for disadvantaged pupils.
- **Illness drives Sussex's excess absence everywhere.** All three
  authorities record more illness absence than England, Brighton and
  Hove most of all. Reduced timetables run above the national
  rate in East and West Sussex.
- **The practice gaps are large and specific.** East Sussex suspends at
  twice Brighton and Hove's rate, and West Sussex uses reduced
  timetables at about twice the national rate.
- **Place matters within the region, but mostly as schools.** Average
  value added runs from
  `r sgn(max(DIST$va))` points in `r DIST$lad[which.max(DIST$va)]` to
  `r sgn(min(DIST$va))` in `r DIST$lad[which.min(DIST$va)]`. But only
  Crawley has a district effect that survives once each school's own
  record is counted.
- **Trusts matter about as much as local authorities,** more for
  disadvantaged pupils and attendance. United Learning runs schools in
  both counties and stands out for results. Ark (Hastings) stands out for
  disadvantaged pupils and attendance. Kemnal (West Sussex) and Aldridge
  (Brighton and Hove) run significantly more absence than their intakes
  predict.
- **In none of the three does the mix of pupils between schools explain
  results.** Attendance, prior attainment, and what happens inside
  particular schools do.

# About this review

The three authority-level documents each apply the published national
models to one authority. This review sets them side by side and adds
the view of Sussex as one system. Two things should be borne in mind:

- **Sussex is not an administrative unit** for schools. Its three
  authorities have their own admissions, school improvement and
  attendance services. "Sussex" here is a lens, not a governing body.
- **Brighton and Hove** is the subject of the Lever report itself. Its
  figures here come from the same models and data.

The methods are described in full in the [East Sussex document](east_sussex.html).

# Sussex's schools

```{r map}
#| fig-cap: "Sussex's 76 state-funded secondary schools, coloured by overall absence in 2024/25, within its thirteen districts. Choose another measure from the menu above the map; circle size is the school's roll. Hover for figures and who runs each school."
map_area(X, GOV, LADS, height = 640)
```

```{r tbl-gov}
#| tbl-cap: "Who ran Sussex's secondary schools in 2024/25."
GOV |>
  mutate(kind = case_when(trust_kind == "Maintained" ~ "Maintained",
                          trust_kind == "Multi-academy trust" ~ "Multi-academy trust",
                          TRUE ~ "Single-academy trust or not recorded")) |>
  count(LANAME, kind) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = kind, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  left_join(GOV |> group_by(LANAME) |>
              summarise(Sponsored = sum(route == "Sponsor-led academy"),
                        Trusts = n_distinct(run_by[trust_kind == "Multi-academy trust"]),
                        Schools = n(), .groups = "drop"), by = "LANAME") |>
  rename(`Local authority` = LANAME) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrrrr")
```

The three authorities run their schools very differently:

- **Brighton and Hove** maintains seven of its ten.
- **West Sussex** maintains nearly half.
- **East Sussex** has most of its schools in
  `r n_distinct(GOV$run_by[GOV$LANAME == "East Sussex" & GOV$trust_kind == "Multi-academy trust"])`
  different multi-academy trusts.

Two trusts, United Learning and the University of Brighton Academies
Trust, ran schools in both counties in 2024/25.

# Three systems in one region

```{r profile-table}
#| tbl-cap: "Sussex and its three authorities against England, 2024/25. Means of school-level figures; ranks among all local authorities (1 = highest)."
row <- function(lab, col, d = 1) {
  f <- function(x) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x)
  rnk <- function(la) { p <- p_at(la)
    if (la == "Sussex") f(p[[col]]) else
      sprintf("%s (%s)", f(p[[col]]), ord(rank(-prof[[col]])[prof$LANAME == la])) }
  tibble(Measure = lab, Sussex = rnk("Sussex"), `East Sussex` = rnk("East Sussex"),
         `West Sussex` = rnk("West Sussex"), `Brighton and Hove` = rnk("Brighton and Hove"),
         England = f(sum(prof[[col]] * prof$schools, na.rm = TRUE) /
                       sum(prof$schools[!is.na(prof[[col]])])))
}
bind_rows(
  row("Attainment 8, all pupils", "att8"),
  row("Attainment 8, disadvantaged", "att8_dis"),
  row("Attainment 8, non-disadvantaged", "att8_non"),
  row("Disadvantage gap (points)", "gap"),
  row("Disadvantaged (FSM6) %", "fsm"),
  row("Overall absence %", "absence"),
  row("Persistent absence %", "persistent"),
  row("Mean KS2 (centred)", "ks2_c", 2),
  row("EAL %", "eal")) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrrr")
```

```{r tbl-model}
#| tbl-cap: "What the national model says about each authority: its own effect once intake and circumstances are accounted for (rank, 1 = best), and whether its standing depends on controlling for absence."
tibble(`Local authority` = LAS) |>
  mutate(`All pupils` = sapply(LAS, function(l) { e <- e_at(l, "All pupils")
           sprintf("%+.1f%% (%s)%s", pct(e$effect), ord(e$rank), ifelse(e$sig, "*", "")) }),
         Disadvantaged = sapply(LAS, function(l) { e <- e_at(l, "Disadvantaged")
           sprintf("%+.1f%% (%s)%s", pct(e$effect), ord(e$rank), ifelse(e$sig, "*", "")) }),
         `Disadvantaged rank: with / without absence control` =
           sapply(LAS, function(l) paste(ord(r27("dis", l, "A-raw")), "/", ord(r27("dis", l, "A-none")))),
         `Absence above intake-predicted` =
           sapply(LAS, function(l) sprintf("%+.2f (%s)", c_at(l)$excess, ord(c_at(l)$rank_excess)))) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrr")
```

`*` marks an effect distinguishable from zero.

Read across the two tables, the three authorities are three distinct
cases:

- **Brighton and Hove** is the strongest on the model: its schools are
  `r ord(e_at("Brighton and Hove", "All pupils")$rank)` in England once
  intake is accounted for. It is also the most dependent on absence: it
  falls from `r ord(r27("dis", "Brighton and Hove", "A-raw"))` to
  `r ord(r27("dis", "Brighton and Hove", "A-none"))` for disadvantaged
  pupils without the absence control, because its absence is the
  `r ord(c_at("Brighton and Hove")$rank_excess)` furthest above its intake
  in England.
- **East Sussex** is in the middle on every measure. Its schools do what
  is expected, and its absence is what its intake predicts.
- **West Sussex** is the reverse of Brighton and Hove: absence is
  ordinary, and its schools sit significantly below expectation for
  disadvantaged pupils
  (`r ord(e_at("West Sussex", "Disadvantaged")$rank)` of
  `r e_at("West Sussex", "Disadvantaged")$n_las`).

# What explains attainment across Sussex {#sec-decomp}

```{r fig-decomp}
#| fig-cap: "Why average Attainment 8 differs from England's, by factor, all school-years 2021/22 to 2024/25, for Sussex as a whole and its three authorities. Approximate Attainment 8 points; the pieces sum to the total printed in each panel."
#| fig-height: 11
fig_decomp(dec, ALL, c("All pupils", "Disadvantaged"))
```

```{r decomp-table}
#| tbl-cap: "The decomposition for Sussex as a whole, in Attainment 8 points."
decomp_table(dec, "Sussex")
```

**Sussex as a whole** is `r pts(-d_tot("Sussex", "All pupils"))` points
below England for all pupils. Its low disadvantage lifts it
(`r sgn(d_get("Sussex", "All pupils", "Disadvantage (% FSM)"), 2)`), and
three things pull it down:

- absence (`r pts(d_get("Sussex", "All pupils", "Absence"), 2)`);
- prior attainment (`r pts(d_get("Sussex", "All pupils", "Prior attainment (KS2)"), 2)`);
- being in the South East (`r pts(d_get("Sussex", "All pupils", "Region"), 2)`).

The three authorities' own effects roughly cancel. Brighton and Hove's
positive effect offsets West Sussex's negative one.

**For disadvantaged pupils** Sussex is
`r pts(-d_tot("Sussex", "Disadvantaged"))` points below England. The
largest single piece is the region
(`r pts(d_get("Sussex", "Disadvantaged", "Region"), 2)`), followed by
absence (`r pts(d_get("Sussex", "Disadvantaged", "Absence"), 2)`) and the
authorities' own effects
(`r pts(d_get("Sussex", "Disadvantaged", "Local authority effect"), 2)`,
mostly West Sussex's).

The regional effect is not something any one authority can change, but
it is real and it is shared. Of England's nine regions, the South East
has the most negative effect for disadvantaged pupils: they do less well
there than equally disadvantaged pupils elsewhere with the same prior
attainment and attendance. That is a regional question as much as a
local one.

# Place: authorities and districts {#sec-place}

```{r fig-caterpillar}
#| fig-cap: "Local authority effects from the published national models, disadvantaged pupils, every authority in England with a 95% interval."
#| fig-height: 5.5
fig_caterpillar(eff, LAS, "Disadvantaged",
                "Brighton and Hove near the top, East Sussex in the middle, West Sussex near the bottom")
```

```{r fig-districts}
#| fig-cap: "Sussex's thirteen districts: each school's value added (mean 2021/22 to 2024/25, small dots) and the district mean (large dots), coloured by authority. Districts marked † have a significant district effect on the published model; only Crawley's (‡) survives once each school's own record is counted, and then only for non-disadvantaged pupils."
#| fig-height: 6
crawley_ns <- DE$focus |> filter(spec == "With a school term", sig) |> pull(lad)
# Brighton and Hove is unitary: its "district" term duplicates its LA
# term, so a district mark would be an artefact
lab_d <- DIST |>
  mutate(mark = paste0(lad, ifelse(`sig_Published specification` & la != "Brighton and Hove", " †", ""),
                       ifelse(lad %in% crawley_ns, "‡", "")))
DE$sussex_va |>
  left_join(lab_d |> select(lad, mark, dmean = va), by = "lad") |>
  mutate(mark = reorder(mark, dmean)) |>
  ggplot(aes(va, mark, colour = LANAME)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.6, position = position_jitter(height = 0.12, seed = 1)) +
  geom_point(aes(x = dmean), size = 4.5, shape = 18) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = AREA_COL, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Value added (Attainment 8 points)", y = NULL,
       title = "Worthing and Lewes at the top, Crawley and Hastings at the bottom") +
  theme_note()
```

```{r tbl-districts}
#| tbl-cap: "Sussex's districts, 2024/25 profile and mean value added over 2021/22 to 2024/25."
DIST |>
  arrange(desc(va)) |>
  transmute(District = lad, Authority = la, Schools = schools,
            `FSM %` = round(fsm, 1), `Absence %` = round(absence, 1), KS2 = round(ks2_c, 1),
            `Att 8` = round(att8, 1), `Att 8 disadv.` = round(att8_dis, 1),
            `Value added` = sprintf("%+.1f", va),
            `Schools below expectation` = paste(below, "of", schools)) |>
  kt(align = "llrrrrrrrl")
```

Value added differs widely between districts, and the two ends tell
different stories:

- **Hastings and Crawley** have the lowest value added, and very
  different intakes. Hastings is Sussex's most disadvantaged district;
  Crawley's disadvantage is near the county average.
- **In Hastings**, the low figure is two schools. With each school's own
  record in the model, no district effect remains.
- **In Crawley**, every school is below expectation, and for
  non-disadvantaged pupils the district effect survives the school term.
  It is the closest thing in Sussex to a genuine place effect.
- **Worthing and Lewes** are at the top. Both have some of the region's
  strongest individual schools, and neither has a district effect once
  those schools are counted.

The lesson is consistent across the region. A district is a useful way
to see where difficulties gather, but in all but one case the
difficulty belongs to particular schools, not to the place.

# Trusts across Sussex {#sec-trusts}

```{r trust-setup}
#| include: false
sx_trusts <- unique(GOV$run_by[GOV$trust_kind == "Multi-academy trust"])
TE <- TR$trusts |> mutate(name = tidy_trust(trust_group)) |> filter(name %in% sx_trusts)
tsd <- function(o, l) TR$vcs |> filter(outcome == o, level == l) |> pull(sd)
sig_names <- function(o, s) TE |> filter(outcome == o, sig, sign(effect) == s) |> pull(name)
```

In 2024/25, `r length(sx_trusts)` multi-academy trusts ran Sussex
secondary schools, most of them one or two schools each. The trust
analysis in the [East Sussex document](east_sussex.html#sec-trusts)
estimates every trust's effect across all its secondary schools in
England. It allows for each school's own record and for whether it was
sponsored. Nationally, a trust moves results by about
`r pp(100 * tsd("All pupils", "trust_group"))`%, about as much as a local
authority, and absence by about
`r pp(100 * tsd("Absence (stage 1)", "trust_group"))`%.

```{r fig-trusts}
#| fig-cap: "The national effect of each trust that ran a Sussex secondary school in 2024/25, with 95% intervals; the number of its schools in the national data is in brackets."
#| fig-height: 8.5
fig_trusts(TE, "A few Sussex trusts stand out nationally; most cannot be told from average")
```

Four of the trusts running Sussex schools stand out nationally:

- **Above average:**
  - for all pupils: `r paste(sig_names("All pupils", 1), collapse = ", ")`;
  - for disadvantaged pupils: `r paste(sig_names("Disadvantaged", 1), collapse = ", ")`.
- **Absence below what their intakes predict:**
  `r paste(sig_names("Absence (stage 1)", -1), collapse = ", ")`.
- **Absence above what their intakes predict:**
  `r paste(sig_names("Absence (stage 1)", 1), collapse = ", ")`.

Most of the rest are small trusts that cannot be separated from their
one or two schools.

Nothing here suggests that academies as a group do better or worse than
maintained schools in Sussex. Nationally, the differences by route are a
percent or two once intake is allowed for. The region's strongest
schools on value added are a mix of maintained schools (St Oscar Romero,
St Richard's, Downlands) and academies (King's Academy Ringmer,
Durrington, Steyning).

# Absence across Sussex {#sec-absence}

```{r fig-abs-series}
#| fig-cap: "Overall absence in state-funded secondary schools, autumn and spring terms, 2016/17 to 2025/26. Sessions-weighted; 2019/20 not collected."
#| fig-height: 5
fig_abs_series(ser, LAS, "Brighton and Hove and East Sussex run well above England; West Sussex tracks it")
```

In autumn and spring `r yr(abs_last)`:

- **Brighton and Hove**: `r pp(s_at("Brighton and Hove", abs_last))`%,
  `r ord(rk_at("Brighton and Hove", abs_last))` highest in England.
- **East Sussex**: `r pp(s_at("East Sussex", abs_last))`%,
  `r ord(rk_at("East Sussex", abs_last))`, falling fast.
- **West Sussex**: `r pp(s_at("West Sussex", abs_last))`%,
  `r ord(rk_at("West Sussex", abs_last))`, close to England's
  `r pp(s_at("England", abs_last))`%.

Only Brighton and Hove's is much above what its intake predicts.

```{r fig-reasons}
#| fig-cap: "Absence by register reason, autumn and spring terms, percentage of possible sessions. The ten largest reasons nationally."
#| fig-height: 5.4
fig_reasons(rs, LAS, paste("Illness is above England's rate in all three authorities,", yr(abs_last)))
```

```{r tbl-practice}
#| tbl-cap: "Three measures of practice: illness absence, reduced timetables and sessions lost to suspension (percentage of possible sessions, latest absence year), and suspensions per 100 pupils (latest exclusions year)."
tibble(Area = c(LAS, "Sussex", "England")) |>
  mutate(Illness = sapply(Area, function(a) pp(r_at(a, "Illness"), 2)),
         `Reduced timetable` = sapply(Area, function(a) pp(r_at(a, "Reduced timetable"), 2)),
         `Suspended (code E)` = sapply(Area, function(a) pp(r_at(a, "Suspended (code E)"), 2)),
         `Suspensions per 100` = sapply(Area, function(a) pp(ex_at(a)))) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrr")
```

The table shows three things:

- **Illness is the shared problem.** It is above England's rate
  everywhere, and in Brighton and Hove by a margin
  (`r pp(r_at("Brighton and Hove", "Illness"), 2)`% against
  `r pp(r_at("England", "Illness"), 2)`%). The published data cannot say
  what lies behind it. All three authorities' own records could, and
  comparing them is the obvious first step.
- **Reduced timetables are West Sussex's outlier**, at
  `r sprintf("%.1f", r_at("West Sussex", "Reduced timetable") / r_at("England", "Reduced timetable"))`
  times England's rate.
- **Suspension is East Sussex's outlier**, at
  `r pp(ex_at("East Sussex"))` per 100 pupils against
  `r pp(ex_at("Brighton and Hove"))` in Brighton and Hove. Neighbouring
  authorities with similar pupils make very different decisions about
  exclusion, which suggests these are choices that can be changed.

# School by school {#sec-schools}

```{r fig-plane}
#| fig-cap: "All 76 Sussex schools on the joint-signal plane, mean over 2021/22 to 2024/25: absence above or below what the intake predicts, against value added with attendance counted in. Grey: every school in England."
#| fig-height: 8
xl <- quantile(js$resid_abs_pp, c(0.005, 0.995)); yl <- quantile(js$vadd_M2, c(0.005, 0.995))
xl <- c(min(xl[1], -4), max(xl[2], 4.5)); yl <- c(min(yl[1], -8), max(yl[2], 9))
ext <- js_sx |> filter(abs(vadd_M2) > 3.5 | abs(resid_abs_pp) > 2.5)
ggplot(js, aes(resid_abs_pp, vadd_M2)) +
  geom_point(colour = LIGHT, size = 0.7, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = GREY) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_point(data = js_sx, aes(fill = LANAME), shape = 21, colour = "white", size = 3.2) +
  geom_text_repel(data = ext, aes(label = SCHNAME), size = 2.6, max.overlaps = 40,
                  segment.colour = GREY, colour = INK) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = AREA_COL, name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = xl, ylim = yl) +
  labs(x = "Absence above what the intake predicts (percentage points)",
       y = "Value added, attendance counted in (Attainment 8 points)",
       title = "Across Sussex, schools that hold attendance tend to add value") +
  theme_note()
```

Across Sussex's schools the two signals move together (correlation
`r sprintf("%.2f", cor(js_sx$resid_abs_pp, js_sx$vadd_M2))`). The
schools furthest out are named.

- **Strongest:** St Oscar Romero (Worthing), St Richard's (Bexhill) and
  King's Academy Ringmer.
- **Weakest:** Thomas Bennett (Crawley), the two Hastings academies, and
  The Littlehampton Academy.

Both Hastings academies have since moved to a new trust.

```{r tbl-top-bottom}
#| tbl-cap: "The ten Sussex schools furthest above and below the national model's expectation, mean value added 2021/22 to 2024/25 (Attainment 8 points), with absence above or below intake."
tb <- js_sx |>
  left_join(GOV |> select(URN, run_by), by = "URN") |>
  arrange(desc(vadd_M2))
bind_rows(head(tb, 10) |> mutate(Group = "Above"), tail(tb, 10) |> mutate(Group = "Below")) |>
  transmute(Group, School = SCHNAME, Authority = LANAME, `Run by (2024/25)` = run_by,
            `Value added` = sprintf("%+.1f", vadd_M2),
            `Absence vs intake` = sprintf("%+.1f", resid_abs_pp)) |>
  kt(align = "llllrr")
```

# Implications for Sussex

1. **Disadvantaged pupils are the regional priority.** All three
   authorities are below England for them. A part of the shortfall is
   regional and shared, and so is the case for working on it together.
2. **Each authority has a different first lever.**
   - *Brighton and Hove:* attendance, and finding out why its absence is
     so far above its intake.
   - *East Sussex:* attendance, prior attainment, and its high suspension
     rate.
   - *West Sussex:* what happens inside its schools for disadvantaged
     pupils, starting with Crawley.

   A single Sussex-wide prescription would fit none of them.
3. **Illness absence is common to all three,** and their combined
   records could show what lies behind it in a way no one authority's
   could.
4. **Practice varies more than intake does.** Suspension in East Sussex
   and reduced timetables in West Sussex are choices made within the
   system, and neighbouring authorities make them differently.
5. **Schools, not structures, carry most of the variation.** Districts
   and trusts matter at the margin. The strongest effects in every
   analysis here belong to individual schools. Learning from the region's
   best schools is the most direct lever available, and those schools
   include maintained schools and academies alike.

# Notes on method {.unnumbered}

Methods and sources are those of the [East Sussex document](east_sussex.html).
"Sussex" figures are means over all 76 schools (for school-level
measures) or sums over their sessions and pupils (for absence and
suspensions). This review is built by `R/17_area_analysis.R`,
`R/18_district_effects.R`, `R/19_trust_effects.R`,
`R/19b_sussex_boundaries.R` and `sussex_review.qmd`.
